title: Same Tree
directAnswer: Two trees are the same if they have identical structure and identical values at every position. Walk both trees in lockstep: at each step both nodes must be null together, or both non-null with equal values and recursively-equal left and right subtrees. The null-handling order matters — check both-null and one-null BEFORE comparing values. O(n) time, O(h) space.

remember.pattern: Parallel (lockstep) DFS comparing two trees node-for-node
remember.formula:
same(p, q):
    if p is null and q is null: return True
    if p is null or q is null: return False   # exactly one null → differ
    return p.val == q.val
       and same(p.left, q.left)
       and same(p.right, q.right)
rules: Handle nulls **first**: both-null → equal; exactly-one-null → not equal. Only then compare `.val`.
Recurse in **parallel** — left-with-left and right-with-right, never crossed (crossing is the Symmetric-Tree problem).
Structure AND values must both match — same shape with different numbers is *not* the same tree.
Short-circuit with `&&` / `and`: the first mismatch ends the comparison early.
Both empty trees are the same tree (return true).
whenToUse: You must check two trees for exact equality of shape and values
Any lockstep traversal of two structures advanced together
A helper inside larger problems (Subtree of Another Tree, Symmetric Tree)
antiSignals: You compare a tree against its own mirror → Symmetric Tree (cross the recursion)
You search one tree for a matching subtree → Subtree of Another Tree (call sameTree at each node)
Only values matter, not structure → serialize and compare strings instead
remember.takeaway: Same Tree is the canonical parallel-DFS: advance two pointers through two trees together, and at each step verify the null pattern matches, the values match, and both subtrees recursively match. It's the equality primitive that Subtree of Another Tree and Symmetric Tree are built on top of.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can write a clean two-pointer recursion over two trees and, critically, order the null checks correctly before dereferencing values.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing p.val before checking that p and q are both non-null (null dereference), or forgetting the 'exactly one null → not equal' case so structurally different trees compare equal.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the three-case null logic crisply, note that this is the building block for Subtree of Another Tree, and contrast it with Symmetric Tree where the recursion is crossed.

problemStatement:
Given the roots of two binary trees `p` and `q`, write a function to check if they are **the same** or not.

Two binary trees are considered the same if they are structurally identical, and the nodes have the same value.
constraints: The number of nodes in both trees is in the range [0, 100]
Two empty trees are considered the same
understanding: Decide whether two trees are exact copies — same shape and same value at every corresponding position. We advance through both trees together; the moment the structure diverges (one node present where the other is null) or a value differs, they are not the same.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are two empty trees the same?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — both null is the base case that returns true.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does structure matter, or only the multiset of values?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Structure matters. [1,2] (2 as left child) and [1,null,2] (2 as right child) hold the same values but are NOT the same tree.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can values be negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — values range down to -10⁴, so don't assume positivity. We only ever test equality, so sign is irrelevant to the logic.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Recursive or iterative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Recursive parallel DFS is cleanest. An iterative version pushes pairs of nodes onto a stack/queue and checks them together — offer it if asked.

examples.explanation: Identical structure and identical values at every node.
Same values but different structure — p has 2 as a left child, q has 2 as a right child.
Same structure but the values differ at the children — left/right values are swapped.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Parallel DFS is the natural primitive; an iterative paired-stack version is the recursion-free equivalent.

approaches.name: Parallel Recursive DFS (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Start and stay here — it's the cleanest solution and the one interviewers expect. Nail the null-check ordering.
hints: You're comparing two trees at once. What if your recursive function took TWO nodes, one from each tree, and advanced through both together?
Before touching values, reason about nulls: if both are null they match here; if exactly one is null the structures already differ.
When both are non-null, the node is equal iff values match AND the left pair matches AND the right pair matches — recurse left-with-left and right-with-right.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each pair of corresponding nodes is compared once, so the work is O(min(n, m)) ≈ O(n) where n is the node count. Recursion depth is the tree height h → O(h) space. A mismatch short-circuits early, only ever making it faster.
approaches.explanation:
Equality of two trees is itself recursive: two trees are equal iff their roots match and their corresponding subtrees are equal. So write a function that takes one node from each tree and advances through both in lockstep.

**Get the null cases right — and in order.** Three situations arise at each step. First, if *both* nodes are null, this position is consistently empty in both trees, so it matches — return true. Second, if *exactly one* is null (checked with `p == null || q == null` after the both-null case), the structures already diverge — return false. Only after those two guards is it safe to dereference `.val`, because both nodes are now guaranteed non-null. Flipping this order — comparing values first — risks a null-pointer exception, and dropping the one-null case makes structurally different trees compare equal.

**The recursive case.** With both nodes non-null, they're equal here iff their values match *and* their left subtrees are equal *and* their right subtrees are equal. The `&&` / `and` short-circuits: the first failing condition stops the comparison, so a mismatch high in the tree never explores the rest.

**Parallel, never crossed.** Compare left-with-left and right-with-right. This is what distinguishes Same Tree from Symmetric Tree — the latter crosses the recursion (left-with-right) to check mirror symmetry. Saying that contrast out loud shows you understand the structure rather than memorizing one snippet.

**Why O(n) is optimal.** In the worst case (identical trees) you must inspect every node to be sure, so no algorithm can do better than linear.
approaches.insight: The whole problem hinges on a tidy three-way null decision made BEFORE any value comparison: both-null is true, one-null is false, both-non-null falls through to the value-and-subtree check. Recite that ladder and the code writes itself — and it's the exact helper you'll reuse inside Subtree of Another Tree.

dryRun.intro: Compare nodes in lockstep. p has 2 as a left child; q has 2 as a right child.

code.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def isSameTree(self, p: TreeNode, q: TreeNode) -> bool:
    if not p and not q:                          # both empty → match
        return True
    if not p or not q:                           # exactly one empty → differ
        return False
    return (p.val == q.val                        # values must match
            and self.isSameTree(p.left, q.left)   # left subtrees match
            and self.isSameTree(p.right, q.right))  # right subtrees match

Every pair matches in value and structure → returns true after visiting all nodes.

pitfalls: Comparing p.val == q.val before the null guards — null-pointer exception when one side is null.
Omitting the 'exactly one null' case — structurally different trees wrongly compare equal.
Crossing the recursion (p.left with q.right) — that solves Symmetric Tree, not Same Tree.

approaches.name: Iterative — Stack/Queue of Node Pairs
approaches.whenToMention: Offer if asked to avoid recursion or if very deep trees could overflow the call stack.
hints: Recursion implicitly pairs nodes. What if you stored those pairs explicitly in a stack or queue and checked them one at a time?
Push the pair (p, q). Pop a pair, apply the same null/value logic; if it passes, push the (left,left) and (right,right) child pairs.
If any popped pair fails the null or value check, return false. If the container empties without a failure, the trees are identical.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each corresponding node pair is pushed and popped once → O(n) time. The container can hold up to O(n) pairs in the worst case (e.g. a wide level), so O(n) space — slightly worse than the recursion's O(h).
approaches.explanation:
The iterative version makes the pairing explicit. Instead of letting recursion match `p`'s node with `q`'s node, we store those pairs in a stack (or queue) and process them manually.

**The loop.** Seed the container with the root pair `(p, q)`. Repeatedly pop a pair and apply the identical three-way logic: both null → consistent, skip; exactly one null → return false; both non-null with differing values → return false. When a pair passes, push its two child pairs `(a.left, b.left)` and `(a.right, b.right)` so they get checked too. If the container drains with no failure, every corresponding position matched → return true.

**Why use it.** Functionally identical to the recursion; the only reason to prefer it is to dodge a deep call stack or because the interviewer explicitly asks for an iterative solution. Note the space is O(n) rather than the recursion's O(h), since the container can hold an entire level of pairs.
approaches.insight: Any parallel recursion can be made iterative by storing the *pairs* that the recursion would have created. The trick is remembering to push child pairs only after the current pair passes its checks — otherwise you'd dereference a null.

dryRun.intro: Stack holds node pairs. Pop, check, push child pairs. Stack shown top-first.

code.python:
def isSameTree(self, p: TreeNode, q: TreeNode) -> bool:
    stack = [(p, q)]
    while stack:
        a, b = stack.pop()
        if a is None and b is None:                  # consistent empty
            continue
        if a is None or b is None:                   # structural mismatch
            return False
        if a.val != b.val:                           # value mismatch
            return False
        stack.append((a.left, b.left))
        stack.append((a.right, b.right))
    return True

java.explanation: Seed with the root pair; each stack entry is a pair of corresponding nodes.
Both empty here — consistent, move on without pushing children.
Safe after the null guards; any value mismatch ends the comparison.
Queue up the corresponding child pair — left with left.

python.explanation: A list of tuples is a natural pair-stack in Python.

python.line: if a is None and b is None: continue
if a is None or b is None: return False

python.explanation: Push the right child pair to be checked later.

edgeCases.behavior: First popped pair is (null,null) → continue → stack empties → true.
The (2, null) child pair triggers the one-null guard → false.
Stack holds at most O(h) pairs here, but O(n) in the worst wide case.

pitfalls: Pushing child pairs before the null/value checks pass — risks dereferencing a null later.
Forgetting `continue` on the both-null case and instead falling through to push nulls indefinitely.
Using a single-node stack instead of pairs — you must track both trees together.

commonMistakes: Dereferencing p.val before confirming both p and q are non-null.
Omitting the 'exactly one null' case so different structures look equal.
Crossing the recursion (left with right), which solves Symmetric Tree instead.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Value comparison before null guards
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If one node is null and you read .val first, you get a NullPointerException / AttributeError. The null cases must be resolved before any dereference.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the one-null case
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without the 'exactly one null' guard, a tree and a structurally different tree (one has a child where the other doesn't) can fall through and wrongly compare equal.

followupVariations.title: Symmetric Tree
followupVariations.hint: Compare a tree against itself but CROSS the recursion: left-with-right and right-with-left.

followupVariations.title: Subtree of Another Tree
followupVariations.hint: Run isSameTree at every node of the big tree to test if the small tree matches there.

followupVariations.title: Invert Binary Tree
followupVariations.hint: The transformation cousin — swap children instead of comparing two trees.

followupVariations.title: Flip Equivalent Binary Trees
followupVariations.hint: Like Same Tree but children may be swapped — try both matched and crossed recursions.

patternNote: Parallel DFS: advance two structures together and compare them position-by-position. The careful three-way null handling (both-null, one-null, both-non-null) is the reusable core. This equality primitive is embedded inside Subtree of Another Tree and twisted (crossed) into Symmetric Tree.
